content:
Generalised osteoarthritis means osteoarthritis in several joints, often the hands, knees, hips and spine.

This guide offers ideas for planning a day around several painful joints. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Planning your day

  • Do important tasks when you usually feel best.
  • Break tasks into smaller steps.
  • Alternate sitting and standing tasks.
  • Plan rests before you need them.

Pacing when several joints hurt

Pacing means keeping activity steady rather than overdoing it on good days and crashing afterwards. An activity diary can help you find a level you can keep up.

Movement

  • Gentle exercise for strength and flexibility, as recommended by NICE.
  • Short walks or seated exercise.
  • A physiotherapist can suggest a programme for several joints.

Equipment and help

An OT can suggest aids for dressing, cooking and washing. Ask your council for a needs assessment if daily tasks are becoming hard.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Is it worth exercising if everything hurts?

Gentle, regular exercise often helps osteoarthritis pain. Start small.

Should I rest on bad days?

Some rest helps, but keeping a little gentle movement is usually better than total rest.
